If you are enrolled in a qualifying High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP), using a Health Savings Account (HSA) is one of the most tax-efficient wealth-building tools available. Why an HSA is worth consideration

An HSA offers a rare triple tax advantage that outpaces traditional retirement accounts:

Tax-free contributions: Contributions reduce your federal taxable income.

Tax-free growth: Any interest or investment gains compound without tax drag.

Tax-free distributions: Withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are never taxed.

Unlike a Flexible Spending Account (FSA), HSA funds never expire. The balance rolls over every year and stays with you even if you switch jobs or retire. After age 65, the account functions much like a traditional IRA: you can withdraw funds for non-medical expenses without penalty (paying only ordinary income tax), while qualified healthcare expenses remain 100% tax-free.

How this applies to your situation

2026 contribution limit: For self-only coverage, the statutory limit is $4,400.

Payroll vs. self-employed contributions: If you contribute via W-2 payroll, your contributions bypass both federal income tax and the 7.65% FICA tax. If you contribute directly using self-employment income, the contribution reduces your adjusted gross income (AGI) on Schedule 1, but it does not reduce self-employment tax. Because Washington does not have a state personal income tax, your savings will come entirely from the federal side.

Your cash cushion: Qualifying as an HDHP in 2026 requires an individual deductible of at least $1,700 and a maximum out-of-pocket limit of $8,500. With $23,700 in liquid cash across your Chase checking and Ally savings accounts, you have the reserves needed to absorb that higher upfront deductible without financial strain.

If you are generally healthy with manageable routine medical costs, pairing an HDHP with a fully funded HSA could help accelerate your long-term savings.

Multi-policy bundling and claims reliability: Pairing home and auto with one insurer often provides multi-policy discounts, but the net bottom-line premium and insurer financial strength (AM Best ratings) matter far more than the discount percentage itself.
